abstract: Pursuing a high catalytic selectivity is challenging but paramount for an efficient and low-cost CO2 electrochemical reduction (CO2R). In this work, we demonstrate a significant correlation between the selectivity of CO2R to formate and the duration of tin (Sn) electrodeposition over cuprous oxide (Cu2O)-derived substrate. A Sn electrodeposition time of 120 s led to a cathode with a formate faradaic efficiency of around 81% at -1.1 V vs. RHE, which was over 37% higher than the Sn foil and the sample treated for 684 s. This result highlights the significant role of the interface between deposited Sn and the cuprous-derived substrate in determining the selectivity of CO2R. High-resolution X-ray photoelectron spectra revealed that residue cuprous species at the Cu/Sn interfaces could stabilize Sn species at oxidation states of 2+ and 4+, a mixture of which is essential for a selective formate conversion. sections.heading: Introduction
sections.text:
The electrochemical CO2 reduction (CO2R) holds promise to mitigate CO2 emissions due to its unparalleled advantages such as mild operating conditions, modulable design, and capability to integrate the existing carbon-intensive industrial processes with renewable energy from wind and solar.1-3 This process can convert CO2 into various valuable products such as CO, HCOO/HCOOH, CH4, C2H4, and alcohols.4-6 Notably, the production of HCOOH from CO2 appears economically feasible because of its low energy demand and relatively high commercial value.7 However, a low product selectivity of CO2R lowers the energy efficiency and increases the complexity of downstream product separation, which consequently leads to a costly overall CO2R process. Therefore, pursuing catalysts that activate selective CO2R is imperative to increase the viability of this technology. Tin (Sn)-based materials are promising catalysts for CO2R to produce formate because of its low material cost, low toxicity and the relatively high selectivity towards formate.8-11 Most of the works,12-13 including our recent work,14 reported a strong dependency of formate selectivity on the oxidation state of Sn. This trend is supported by Baruch et al.15, who used an in-situ infrared spectroscopy measurement to reveal that the CO2R over Sn metal surface likely proceeds via a surface-bound carbonate (*OCHO intermediate) interacting with Sn (II) oxyhydroxide species. Dutta et al. also observed a strong correlation between the oxidation states of tin oxide nanoparticles and FE to formate via time- and potential- resolved in-situ Raman characterization.16 Through combined density functional theory calculations and experimental investigations, An et al. 17 unveiled that the Sn4+ reduces overpotentials, Sn2+ promotes formate production, and oxide/metal interfaces suppress unwanted HER. Many strategies have been proposed to enhance the formate selectivity of Sn-based catalysts, including introducing heterogeneous atoms and optimizing particle size and morphologies10, 18- 22. For example, Zheng et al.19, 23 demonstrated an excellent formate selectivity up to 93% - 95% over a slightly-oxidized Sn as imparted by Cu or sulphur. Liang et al.24 reported an ultrasmall SnO2 that achieved a peak faradaic efficiency of formate at 74% at -0.73 V vs. reversible hydrogen electrode (RHE). In addition to chalcogenide23, 25 and oxide-derivation10, 12, another

3 effective strategy to control the oxidation state of transition metals is to control the electronegativity difference between active metal sites and their neighboring dopants. This strategy has been well exemplified by our previous work at UQ to develop metal oxide-based electrode catalysts for fuel cell applications.26-28 Note that Cu+ has an electronegativity of 1.56 that falls in between 1.73 for Sn4+ and 1.34 for Sn2+.29 Mistry et al.30 reported that the cuprous species exist on oxide-derived copper surfaces during CO2R. Under CO2R potentials, this electronegativity difference could allow Cu+ to stabilize oxidation states of Sn because the presence of Cu+ (electronegativity of 1.56) can donate electrons to Sn4+ at electronegativity of 1.73, but Cu+ can accept electrons from Sn2+ at 1.34.29 In this work, we oxidized Cu foils to produce a Cu2O layer on the foils and then used chronopotentiometric electrodeposition to deposit Sn catalyst on the Cu2O-derived layer. We observed a strong correlation between the electrodeposition time, which increased the Sn coverage over the Cu2O-derived substrate and affected the area of the Sn/Cu interfaces, and the selectivity of the cathode for CO2R to formate. Our analysis of the surface composition, oxidation states, and morphology of the Sn/Cu2O-derived electrodes revealed that deposition time and consequently the Sn/Cu2O-derived interfaces affect the oxidation state of Sn atoms on the surface and therefore the catalyst’s selectivity for CO2R to formate. This modulation effect likely arises from the electronegativity of Cu+ that is lower than that of Sn4+ but higher than that of Sn2+,29 and balances the exposure of Sn2+/Sn4+ at the surface. This work demonstrated that an optimal catalyst deposition time exists to achieve a selective CO2R, and highlighted the essential role of catalyst substrate in determining the selectivity of the catalysts.

sections.heading: Materials preparation
sections.text:
Copper foils (0.5 mm, ≥ 99.99%, Sigma Aldrich) were polished with the diamond polishing solution (ALS-Japan) to a mirror finish, then rinsed with deionized water and ethanol, and sonicated for 15 min in 0.5 M H2SO4 and then in deionized water. We refer to the polished foil as fresh Cu. The surface of the fresh Cu foils was oxidized to a layer of the Cu2O by immersing the Cu foil in a stirred chemical bath of 0.668 M Na2SnO3 (95%, Sigma Aldrich) and 0.375 M NaOH (≥ 98 %, Sigma Aldrich) at 55°C for 30 minutes. Then we electrodeposited Sn onto the oxidized Cu surface from the Na2SnO3 + NaOH solution at an applied current density of 72 mA cm-2, using a Pt foil counter electrode and Ag|AgCl (3M NaCl) (from ALS Japan) reference electrode. We controlled the electrodeposition time to be 20 s, 30 s, 60 s, 120 s, 240 s, and

The area of the electrode was around 1.5-2.5 cm2, and the exact area of each electrode was recorded.

sections.heading: Electrochemical measurement
sections.text:
We performed the CO2R experiments using a three-electrode configuration in an H-type electrochemical cell with a Nafion 117 separator (from FuelCellStore) in similar procedures to what we have described elsewhere.31 The working electrode (e.g., fresh Cu, 0 s sample, Sn on Cu2O, or Sn foil) was sonicated in deionized water for 2 min and then immediately immersed in 70 mL of 0.5 M KHCO3 solutions in the cathode chamber of the H-cell with an Ag|AgCl (3M NaCl) reference electrode. A 0.6 cm diameter graphite rod (Sigma-Aldrich) was used as the counter-electrode in 30 ml of 0.5 M KHCO3 in the anode chamber. The cell was prepared for CO2R experiments by first purging the electrolytes with Ar and then purging the catholyte with CO2 (99.999%, Supagas Australia) for at least 30 min. All CO2R tests were performed at room temperature and ambient pressure and controlled by a using Metrohm Autolab PGSTAT302N potentiostat. The pH and temperature of the catholyte were measured continuously with a Metrohm LL Unitrode PT1000 probe. During CO2R experiments, CO2 was continuously bubbled through the catholyte at 30 sccm using a mass flow controller (MKS Instruments, ± 1% resolution). The catholyte and anolyte were each continuously stirred at 500 rpm. sections.text:
Gas products from CO2R were analyzed using a Shimadzu GC-2030 gas chromatograph with a ShinCarbon packed column (ST 80/100, 2 mm ID, 1/8 OD Silco, Restek) and a thermal conductivity detector (TCD) and a flame ionization detector (FID). Argon (Ar, 99.999%, Supagas Australia) and hydrogen (H2, 99.999% BOC Australia) were used as the carrier gas for the TCD and the FID, respectively, with zero air as the balance gas for the FID. We estimated the electrochemically-active surface area of cathodes in the H-cell by performing cyclic voltammetric (CV) analysis at voltage scan rates between 0.01 and 0.09 V s-1 over a 0.1 V electrochemical window in the non-Faradaic region in a CO2-saturated 0.5 M KHCO3 aqueous solution. The scan rates for the CVs were controlled in the range. The double-layer capacitances were calculated from the slopes of the capacitive current at open circuit potential vs. the scan rate, as derived from the cyclic voltammetry results. Subsequently, we divided the capacitance by 0.029 mF cm-2, which is widely believed to be the specific capacitance for Sn-based materials.19

sections.heading: Results and Discussions
sections.text:
The X-ray diffraction spectra in Figure 1A, and inset for 2θ in the range of 34 - 65 degrees, shows a layer of Cu2O on the surface of the polished Cu foil that was soaked for 30 minutes in the 0.668 M Na2SnO3 and 0.375 M NaOH aqueous solution. The XRD patterns indicate that the major facets of this Cu2O phase are (111), (200), and (220).32 After the 30 min of soaking treatment, we also observed by scanning electron micrograph (SEM) that the smooth surface of the polished Cu foil (Figure 1B) became rougher with 300-500 nm sized particles uniformly covering the surface of the soaked Cu (0s) sample (Figure 1C). The formation of the Cu2O layer is consistent with previous reports by MacKay et al.33 and Zhang et al.34.

We used the modified Auger parameter, which is the sum of the kinetic energy of the Cu LMM Auger peaks (Figure 2A) and the binding energy of the Cu 2p3/2 peak (Figure 2B), to distinguish the Cu+ and metallic Cu. Table 1 shows the fresh Cu foil exhibited two modified Auger parameters at 1851.2 eV corresponding to metallic Cu and 1849.2 eV corresponding to Cu+ species.35 The latter Cu+ species observed on fresh Cu is likely due to exposure of the polished foil to the air during handling and transfer to the XPS instrument. After soaking in the Na2SnO3 + NaOH solution for 30 minutes, only the modified Auger parameter 1848.9 eV of Cu+ was observed, which suggests the surface of the Cu foil was completely oxidized to Cu+based species. These XPS interpretations are consistent with the XRD (Figure 1A) and particles observed in the SEM (Figure 1C). We also examined how the surface chemistry of the soaked Cu foil changes after subject to CO2R reaction conditions by using this foil as a cathode at -0.8 V, -1.0 V, and -1.2 V vs. RHE in a CO2-saturated 0.5 M KHCO3 solution for 20 min. The Sn particles were deposited onto the surface of the soaked Cu 0 s sample after only 20 s deposition (shown in Figure 3A). The size of the Sn particles grew to approximately 100 nm (Figure 3B) after a 30 s deposition time. The surface of the 30 s sample became smoother as a result of the growth of the Sn nuclei. The Cu nanoparticles have a higher density of low-coordinated sites such as corners and edges that can bind more strongly with adatoms than the flat surfaces.37 These particles also exhibit a high electric field due to their high curvature.38 Both could lead the Sn to deposit onto the formed Cu2O-derived nanoparticles. The Sn nuclei deposited at the Cu particles started to coarsen between 30 s and 60 s (Figure 3D), and formed a continuous layer to fully cover the Cu foil surface after 120 s deposition time (Figure 3E). A longer deposition time than 120 s led to a formation of a prism-shaped microstructure on top of the continuous layer. (Figure 3F)

the surface when the deposition time is shorter than 120 s. This result is also consistent with
what we observed in SEM micrographs in Figure 3 and EDS mapping in Figure 4. Overall, the
coverage of Cu decreases with deposition time increasing from 20s/30s to 60s. The higher
concentration of Cu in the 30 s sample than 20 s highlights the discontinued Sn layer that may
cause local variations of Cu/Sn dispersion at the surface. Figure 6C shows an illustration of the
processes for Sn electrodeposition over Cu2O-derived substrate.

Considering the unique electronegativity of Cu+ (1.56) that is between 1.73 for Sn4+ and 1.34
for Sn2+,29 we postulated that the cuprous species formed from soaking treatment effects the
oxidation state of Sn atoms on the surface. The less electronegative Cu+ than Sn4+ prevents the
oxidation of surface Sn from 4+ through donating electrons to its neighboring Sn atoms, while
the Cu+ atoms withdraw electrons when Sn is in +2 state due to its relatively high
electronegativity. Such phenomena can be well exemplified by the Sn deposited for 20 s, 30 s,
60 s, and 120 s, as presented in Figure 7B, where the area of contact interface between surface
Sn and Cu is sufficient. For samples with longer deposition time than 120 s, most of the Sn
surface layer is in contact with Sn species and thus are not significantly affected by the Cu
substrate.
The electrodes were evaluated in a custom-made H-cell with a proton-conducting Nafion® 117
membranes separating the cathode and anode chambers. The samples were tested at the cathode
chamber in a CO2-saturated 0.5 M KHCO3 electrolyte. Cyclic voltammograms over 30 s – deposited Sn electrode (Figure S5) showed that the current density in 0.5M KHCO3 saturated with CO2 is higher than that in Ar-saturated electrolyte, suggesting that CO2R occurred at the electrode surface. The major products from the test include formate (HCOO-), CO, and H2, and the total measured overall FE of these products are within 90% - 100%. We detected a small
amount of CH4 (FE <0.5%) and C2H4 (FE< 0.3%) at - 0.8V vs. RHE for 20 s, 30 s, and 60 s deposited Sn, and the FEs of these two products decrease with the Sn electrodeposition time.

We compared the faradaic efficiency (FE, shown in Figure 8A-C) and partial current density
(PCD, shown in Figure 8D-F) of formate (i.e., HCOO-), CO and H2 over the 30 s-deposited Sn electrode with over the Cu foil, 0 s sample, and Sn foil electrodes. As shown in Figure 8A, the
deposited Sn electrode shows a much higher FE of HCOO- than Cu foil and 0 s sample. This
highlights the essential role of deposited Sn species in the formation of HCOO-. Interestingly,
the deposited Sn exhibits a more selective CO2 conversion to formate, especially at a more negative potential. For example, the deposited Sn electrode shows an FEHCOO- of ~ 75%, much higher than that over Sn foil (FEHCOO- = 55%) at -1.1 V vs. RHE. The FECO is the lowest for both Sn-based electrodes and shows the negligible difference between deposited Sn and Sn
foil. (Figure 8B) Additionally, the deposited Sn electrode is more useful to suppress the
unwanted HER, as evidenced by the lowest FE(H2) shown in Figure 8C. Correspondingly, the PCD of HER over the Sn deposited electrode is also the lowest among all the tested electrodes.
The overall FE for CO2R to produce C1 products, including HCOO- and CO product, is ~ 80% over Sn deposited electrode, more than one third higher than the FE(C1) over Sn foil.
The FEHCOO- of the 30 s sample is also higher than the reported values over Cu-Sn alloys, including Cu3Sn (FEHCOO- = ~ 40% at -1.09 V vs. RHE)41 and Cu76Sn24 (FEHCOO- = ~ 54% at - 1.1 V vs. RHE)42. The higher FEHCOO- over the 30 s Sn-deposited sample than over Cu-Sn alloy means that the Cu3Sn alloy phase is not the key active sites for the selective CO2R catalysis. The effective promotion of formate and suppression of the HER likely arises from the Sn/SnOx
interfaces, which was also recently reported by An et al.17 As aforementioned, 30 s-deposited
Sn has sufficient contact with the nanostructured surface of the 0 s sample where Cu+ species
are present. Due to the unique electronegativity of Cu+, the Cu+ stabilizes the oxidation state
of the surface Sn majorly in +2, which was also confirmed by the XPS result shown in Figure
6D.

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text:
In summary, we deposited Sn onto the Cu2O-derived surface for varied deposition durations and evaluated them as the cathode electrodes to catalyze CO2 electrochemical reduction to produce formate in an H-cell. Although the Sn is the major contributor to the formate
production, only a relatively short deposition duration of less than 120 s leads to a selective
formate conversion and suppressed the hydrogen evolution reaction. This result highlights the
significant role of the Cu2O-derived substrate in determining the catalytic selectivity over deposited Sn catalyst. The results of our surface analysis revealed that the Cu+ likely exist at
the surface or at the subsurface during the cathodic Sn deposition and CO2R due to kinetic limitations at the surface. Cu+ has a moderate electronegativity higher than Sn2+ but lower than
Sn4+. When the deposition duration is below 120 s where there is sufficient contact interface

between Sn and Cu, the remaining Cu+ species can stabilize the surface Sn at a relatively
positive oxidation state between +2 and +4 through donating charge to Sn4+ and withdrawing
charge from Sn2+. Such a unique modulation effect of the Cu+ in the substrate contributed to
the observed improved catalytic selectivity over the Sn-deposited electrode. Our work also
highlights the significant roles of the substrate on the electrocatalytic selectivity of the catalyst
and provides an effective alternative strategy to advance selective electrocatalysis by
engineering the substrate.
